items.q: Which otoscopic finding best diagnoses acute otitis media?
o: Bulging opaque drum with lost landmarks
items.exp: Bulging from pus under pressure is the diagnostic sign of AOM. Redness alone occurs with crying and fever, fluid levels mark effusion, and perforation indicates a later ruptured stage.
r: Incorrect. Redness alone is non specific in crying children.
Correct. Bulging opaque drum diagnoses acute otitis media.
Incorrect. That is effusion without acute infection.
Incorrect. Perforation is rupture after AOM, not its defining sign.
items.kp: Bulge makes the diagnosis, not blush.

items.q: Glue ear in a 4 year old persisting 4 months with 30 dB loss and speech delay needs what next?
items.exp: Bilateral effusion beyond three months with hearing and developmental impact meets criteria for audiology and ventilation tube discussion. Antibiotics and drops do not clear chronic effusion.
r: Incorrect. Antibiotics do not resolve established glue ear.
Correct. Test hearing and consider grommets.
Incorrect. Years of deafness harm speech development.
Incorrect. Drops cannot reach fluid behind intact drum.
items.kp: Three months of deaf glue ear: test and tube.

items.q: Unilateral otitis media with effusion in a 55 year old man mandates which examination?
items.exp: Adult unilateral effusion suggests Eustachian tube orifice obstruction, classically nasopharyngeal carcinoma, requiring direct nasopharyngeal inspection and imaging as indicated.
r: Incorrect. Audiogram confirms loss but misses the cause.
Correct. Examine the nasopharynx for obstructing tumour.
Incorrect. Mastoid films do not find nasopharyngeal lesions.
Incorrect. Allergy does not explain unilateral adult effusion.
items.kp: One sided adult glue ear: look at the nasopharynx.

items.q: Most common bacterial cause of acute otitis media in children is which organism group?
items.exp: Pneumococcus, non typable Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis from the nasopharynx cause most childhood AOM. Pseudomonas belongs to canal and chronic perforated disease.
r: Incorrect. Pseudomonas causes otitis externa and chronic discharge.
Correct. Pneumococcus and Haemophilus dominate AOM.
Incorrect. Staph causes canal furuncles mainly.
Incorrect. Anaerobes feature in chronic mastoid disease.
items.kp: Child middle ear bugs come from the nasopharynx.

items.q: A grommet (ventilation tube) helps glue ear by what mechanism?
o: Ventilating middle ear bypassing Eustachian tube
items.exp: Tubes equalise middle ear pressure and drain effusion through the drum while patent, restoring hearing until natural extrusion. They do not medicate or permanently seal the drum.
r: Incorrect. Tubes ventilate; they are not drug devices.
Correct. Ventilation bypasses the failing Eustachian tube.
Incorrect. The hole closes after extrusion usually.
Incorrect. Adenoidectomy is a separate operation.
items.kp: Grommets are vents, not medicine ports.

items.q: Recurrent acute otitis media is defined approximately as what?
o: Three in 6 months or four in a year
items.exp: Three episodes in six months or four in twelve months (with one recent) define recurrent AOM prompting referral, hearing checks and preventive measures. Single perforation alone does not define it.
r: Incorrect. Two in two years is ordinary childhood frequency.
Correct. Three in six or four in twelve months.
Incorrect. One ruptured episode is severity, not recurrence pattern.
Incorrect. Effusion surveillance is glue ear follow up.
items.kp: Three in six, four in twelve: recurrent.

items.q: Why does AOM perforation often relieve the child's pain abruptly?
o: Pus drainage releases middle ear pressure
items.exp: Bulging pus under pressure causes severe pain; spontaneous perforation vents pus, relieving pain while otorrhoea begins. Infection still needs follow up and drum healing checks.
r: Incorrect. Drainage relieves pressure; infection persists initially.
Correct. Venting pus drops pressure and pain.
Incorrect. Healing takes days to weeks after.
Incorrect. Relief tracks drainage mechanically.
items.kp: Pop and drain: pressure off, pain off.

items.q: Tympanometry in glue ear typically shows which pattern?
o: Flat type B curve with normal canal volume
Flat curve with huge canal volume
items.exp: Fluid filled middle ear cannot comply, giving flat type B tympanogram with normal canal volume (intact drum). Large volume flat curve instead suggests perforation or patent tube.
r: Incorrect. Peaked curve is normal aerated ear.
Correct. Flat B with normal volume means effusion.
Incorrect. Huge volume means open perforation or tube.
Incorrect. Hypermobile curves occur in flaccid drums or ossicular discontinuity.
items.kp: Flat B, normal volume: fluid. Flat B, huge volume: hole.

items.q: Which measure does NOT help recurrent childhood otitis media prevention?
items.exp: Decongestants and antihistamines show no benefit for otitis media prevention or effusion clearance. Smoke avoidance, vaccination and breastfeeding reduce risk modestly.
r: Incorrect. Smoke exposure raises recurrence; avoiding helps.
Incorrect. Vaccination reduces pneumococcal episodes.
Correct. Decongestants do not prevent otitis media.
Incorrect. Breastfeeding is protective.
items.kp: Sprays and syrups do not keep ears clear.

items.q: Adenoidectomy aids glue ear mainly in which selected children?
o: Older children with adenoid hypertrophy and nasal obstruction
items.exp: Adenoidectomy benefits selected older children where enlarged adenoids obstruct the nasopharynx and Eustachian orifices, often combined with tube surgery on recurrence. It is not routine for infants.
r: Incorrect. Infants are not candidates for this indication.
Correct. Older children with obstructive adenoids benefit.
Incorrect. Perforation is chronic suppurative disease pathway.
Incorrect. Adult effusion needs tumour exclusion first.
items.kp: Big blocking adenoids in older children: removal helps ears.
